Roll her onto her left side or manually displace the uterus to the left
Administer an antiemetic
quiz.why: The gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when supine, cutting venous return. Left lateral positioning or manual left uterine displacement relieves it within seconds. Leg elevation does not remove the compression, sitting upright is unnecessary, and an antiemetic treats a symptom rather than the cause.

quiz.q: A 27-year-old with no diabetes history has a glucose of 186 mg/dL after a motor vehicle collision. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Newly diagnosed diabetes requiring insulin now
Evidence of diabetic ketoacidosis
A sign that the patient is not seriously injured
Stress hyperglycemia from epinephrine and cortisol
quiz.why: Both stress hormones raise glucose deliberately to fuel the response, so values of 150–200 mg/dL are common and expected in significant trauma. It says nothing reassuring about injury severity, and DKA would require ketones, acidosis and a very different clinical picture.

quiz.q: A patient on prednisone 10 mg daily for rheumatoid arthritis arrives with vomiting, BP 78/44, sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 5.9 mEq/L and glucose 58 mg/dL, and does not improve after 2 L of fluid. What is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: Adrenal crisis
Anaphylaxis
Neurogenic shock
Diabetic ketoacidosis
quiz.why: The combination of fluid-unresponsive hypotension, low sodium, high potassium and low glucose in a chronically steroid-treated patient is the classic adrenal crisis pattern, and hydrocortisone is the treatment. Anaphylaxis would show urticaria and airway involvement, neurogenic shock follows cord injury, and DKA raises rather than lowers glucose.

quiz.q: Which change happens earliest as the body defends volume during hemorrhage?
choices: Falling systolic blood pressure
Falling urine output as aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone conserve salt and water
Falling body temperature
Falling respiratory rate
quiz.why: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and antidiuretic hormone conserve salt and water at the kidney very early, so urine output falls well before blood pressure. Temperature is not a volume marker, and respiratory rate typically rises rather than falls.

quiz.q: Cortisol is described as having a permissive effect on blood pressure. What does that mean?
choices: Cortisol is itself a powerful direct vasoconstrictor
Cortisol permits fluid to shift into the vessels from cells
Cortisol allows blood vessels to respond normally to catecholamines
Cortisol permits the kidney to excrete potassium
quiz.why: Cortisol does not raise pressure much on its own, but without it vessels respond poorly to epinephrine and norepinephrine, which is exactly why adrenal crisis produces hypotension refractory to fluids and pressors. It does not directly shift intracellular water into the vessels.

quiz.q: A hospitalized patient's temperature is charted as 36.3 C at 04:30 and 37.4 C at 17:00 on the same day. What does this most likely represent?
choices: Two different thermometers producing conflicting values
Developing hypothermia overnight
An intermittent fever pattern requiring cultures
A normal circadian swing of roughly 0.5 C between the early-morning trough and afternoon peak
quiz.why: Core temperature is physiologically lowest around 04:00–05:00 and highest in the late afternoon, and a roughly 0.5 C spread is expected. Neither value crosses a fever or hypothermia threshold, and the pattern alone does not indicate infection.

quiz.q: Which nap strategy best avoids sleep inertia during a night shift?
choices: A 45-minute nap
A 20-minute nap, or a full 90-minute cycle if time allows
A 60-minute nap
Any nap taken between 03:00 and 05:00
quiz.why: Slow-wave sleep begins around 30 minutes, and waking out of it produces heavy grogginess. Twenty minutes stays above it and a 90-minute cycle finishes past it; 45 and 60 minutes both land in the worst window. Nap timing alone does not solve the inertia problem.

quiz.q: A clinician has been awake for 22 hours. What is the best evidence-informed statement about their performance?
choices: Performance is unaffected as long as they feel alert
Caffeine fully restores baseline performance
Only physical coordination is affected, not judgment
Performance is impaired comparably to significant alcohol intoxication, and self-assessment of that impairment is unreliable
quiz.why: Around 17–19 hours awake produces impairment comparable to a blood alcohol concentration near 0.05%, and roughly 24 hours approaches 0.10%. Crucially, the ability to judge one's own impairment degrades along with performance, and caffeine masks sleepiness without restoring accuracy.

quiz.q: A patient who works nights complains of weight gain and poor sleep despite eight hours in bed each day. Which mechanism most likely contributes?
choices: Circadian misalignment with raised ghrelin and lowered leptin
Excess slow-wave sleep during daytime hours
Increased melatonin production during the day
Improved insulin sensitivity from shift work
quiz.why: Short and misaligned sleep raises the hunger hormone ghrelin and lowers the satiety hormone leptin, and circadian misalignment worsens rather than improves insulin sensitivity. Daylight suppresses rather than increases melatonin, which is why daytime sleep is lighter and more fragmented.

quiz.q: A burn patient 8 hours post-injury has extensive edema, HR 132 and BP 88/56. Which statement best explains the hemodynamics?
choices: The edema proves the patient has received too much fluid
Damaged capillaries leak plasma into tissue, so the patient is swollen and intravascularly depleted at once
Burns cause cardiogenic shock through direct myocardial injury
Edema and hypotension cannot coexist
quiz.why: Burn injury produces massive capillary leak, third-spacing plasma into tissue. Visible swelling and intravascular depletion happen together, which is why burn resuscitation gives large volumes to a patient who already looks waterlogged.

quiz.q: Which pair of findings together should most strongly raise suspicion for sepsis in a 90-year-old?
choices: Temperature 39.2 C and heart rate 128
New confusion and a respiratory rate of 24 at a temperature of 36.2 C
Blood pressure 158/88 and a dry cough
Chest pain radiating to the left arm
quiz.why: Immunosenescence blunts fever and tachycardia, so the geriatric sepsis signal is altered mental status plus tachypnea, which are two of the three qSOFA elements. The classic febrile tachycardic picture is real when present but far less common in this age group.

quiz.q: A patient with a serum lactate of 5.2 mmol/L improves to 3.1 mmol/L after three hours of treatment. What does this indicate?
choices: Lactate clearance well above the 10% target, suggesting the resuscitation is working
Treatment failure, since the value remains above normal
The original value was erroneous
No conclusion can be drawn without a repeat blood pressure
quiz.why: A 40% drop far exceeds the usual 10% clearance target and suggests improving tissue perfusion. The value is still abnormal and treatment continues, but the trend is the useful information, and clearance is interpreted independently of the pressure.

scenarios.title: ED: 68F, three days of vomiting and now too weak to stand
scenarios.intro: Triage hands you a 68-year-old woman brought in by her daughter. Three days of vomiting after a family dinner, nothing staying down, no diarrhea. She has not urinated since yesterday morning. Past history: hypertension on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide, and osteoarthritis. She is awake and answering, but slowly, and her daughter says she is normally sharp.

steps.prompt:
You have her on the stretcher. She is pale, her lips are dry and cracked, and her tongue looks furrowed. She says she feels dizzy whenever she sits up. Her daughter is asking whether this is just a stomach bug.

What do you do first?

choices.text: Take a full set yourself including a manual pressure, look at skin and capillary refill, and get a glucose
choices.feedback: Correct. The machine pressure of 104/82 has a pulse pressure of 22, which is the finding that matters here. Confirming it manually and adding skin, refill and a glucose takes under two minutes and reframes the whole case.

choices.text: Test skin turgor on the back of her hand and chart the result as your hydration assessment
choices.feedback: Weak. Aging skin loses elastin and tents regardless of hydration, so turgor gives false positives in this age group. Mucous membranes, urine output and orthostatic change are the usable signs.

choices.text: Reassure the daughter it is likely viral and place the patient in the waiting area for a bed
choices.feedback: Harmful. A narrow pulse pressure, tachycardia and anuria for over 24 hours describe compensated hypovolemic shock, not a stomach bug. This patient loses ground while she waits.

choices.text: Have her stand for orthostatic vital signs right now
choices.feedback: Poor choice. She is already tachycardic with a narrow pulse pressure and reports dizziness on sitting up. You have your answer, and standing her up can only produce a fall.

steps.prompt:
Manual pressure confirms `102/84`. Capillary refill is `4` seconds, hands are cool, glucose is `118 mg/dL`. She has produced no urine since arrival.

The resident asks you what the pulse pressure tells her. What is your answer?

choices.text: A pulse pressure of 18 means the arterioles are clamped down to defend pressure: compensated hypovolemia
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Normal is 30–40 mmHg. A diastolic climbing toward the systolic is vasoconstriction at work, and it appears well before the systolic falls.

choices.text: It is not clinically useful; only the systolic matters
choices.feedback: Wrong, and this is the exact error the case is built around. The systolic of 102 is the reassuring number that hides the problem. The pulse pressure is where the information lives.

choices.text: A narrow pulse pressure suggests vasodilation and probable sepsis
choices.feedback: Backwards. Vasodilation produces a WIDE pulse pressure with warm flushed skin. Narrow with cold skin is clamped vessels and volume loss.

choices.text: It reflects her chronic hypertension and her home antihypertensives
choices.feedback: Not the best reading. Her medications are relevant, but they do not produce a 4-second capillary refill, cool hands and anuria. Those findings are perfusion findings.

steps.prompt:
A lactate comes back at `4.3 mmol/L`. Sodium is `149 mEq/L`. The attending is deciding how aggressively to treat.

How do you present the lactate?

choices.text: Lactate 4.3 with a systolic over 100 is cryptic shock and carries high mortality despite the pressure
choices.feedback: Correct, and this is the point of the case. A lactate at or above 4.0 mmol/L identifies tissue hypoperfusion the blood pressure is hiding, and it argues for aggressive resuscitation now.

choices.text: Lactate is only meaningful when the patient is hypotensive, so it can be repeated later
choices.feedback: Wrong in the most consequential direction. The entire value of lactate is that it sees past a normal pressure. Waiting for hypotension means waiting for decompensation.

choices.text: The sodium of 149 shows she lost more water than salt, which fits vomiting plus a thiazide and insensible loss
choices.feedback: A good and accurate observation about the type of loss, which will shape fluid choice. But it is not the most urgent thing to say, because the lactate is the mortality signal.

choices.text: Lactate is nonspecific, so it should be disregarded here
choices.feedback: Too dismissive. Lactate does rise from seizures, albuterol, metformin and liver failure, but none of those is present, and a value of 4.3 always demands an explanation.

steps.prompt:
She receives isotonic fluid. Two hours later you repeat the numbers and a second lactate.

Heart rate `96`, blood pressure `118/72`, capillary refill `2` seconds, and she has put out `140 mL` of urine. The repeat lactate is `2.4 mmol/L`.

What is the correct interpretation?

choices.text: Lactate clearance of about 44%, well above the 10% target, and the pulse pressure has widened to 46: she is responding
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. Clearance above 10% suggests the resuscitation is working, and the widening pulse pressure means the arterioles are releasing their grip because they no longer need to clamp.

choices.text: The lactate is still above 2.0, so nothing has improved
choices.feedback: Too rigid. The trend is the information. A 44% drop alongside restored urine output and normal capillary refill is a clear response, and treatment continues toward full normalization.

choices.text: She is now fluid overloaded and needs a diuretic
choices.feedback: Harmful. Nothing here suggests overload: no crackles, no distended neck veins, and urine output has only just resumed. A diuretic would undo the resuscitation.

choices.text: The improvement proves the original lactate was a laboratory error
choices.feedback: No. A value that falls in response to treatment is behaving exactly as a true lactate should. An erroneous value would not track the clinical course.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern to carry out of this case is that the blood pressure was never the useful number. A systolic of 102 sat inside the normal range the whole time while a pulse pressure of 18, a capillary refill of 4 seconds, anuria and a lactate of 4.3 all said the same thing: this patient was in compensated hypovolemic shock.

Three specific habits did the work. Reading the pulse pressure rather than the systolic. Recognizing that a lactate at or above 4.0 mmol/L identifies hypoperfusion the cuff cannot see. And using a repeat lactate as the scoreboard, where a drop of at least 10% says the plan is working.

The sodium of 149 added the mechanism: vomiting plus a thiazide plus insensible loss took more water than salt, which is hypotonic loss. And skin turgor, the test most people reach for first, was the one finding that would have told you nothing in a 68-year-old.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 81M found on the bathroom floor, unclear how long
scenarios.intro: Dispatch: 81-year-old male, found down by a neighbor who had not seen him in two days. Unlocked door. The house is cold; the neighbor says the heat has been out since the weekend. Medications visible on the counter include metoprolol, warfarin, and prednisone 10 mg daily.

steps.prompt:
He is on the tile floor in a thin shirt, awake but confused, oriented to person only. His neighbor says he is normally sharp and lives alone without help. Skin is cool and dry to your hand.

Your partner says the vitals look basically fine. What is your response?

choices.text: Point out that on metoprolol at age 81 the heart rate cannot be trusted, and the confusion plus RR 22 plus temp 35.4 is the real signal
choices.feedback: Correct. Beta blockade plus age-blunted sympathetic response removes tachycardia as a warning sign. New confusion and tachypnea are two qSOFA elements, and a low temperature is on the SIRS list precisely because sick older patients run cold.

choices.text: Agree that the numbers are reassuring and focus on getting him warm and comfortable
choices.feedback: Dangerous. Warming him is right, but treating these vitals as reassuring ignores that his warning systems are pharmacologically and physiologically disabled. The confusion is the vital sign here.

choices.text: Note the low temperature and treat this purely as environmental hypothermia
choices.feedback: Partly right and incomplete. The cold house is real, but a temperature of 35.4 C in an older adult can equally be sepsis presenting without fever. Both need to stay on the list.

choices.text: Attribute the confusion to age and dementia and move on
choices.feedback: Harmful. The neighbor explicitly said he is normally sharp. New confusion in an older adult is an acute finding until someone proves otherwise, never a baseline assumption.

steps.prompt:
Glucose is `62 mg/dL`. He has a large bruise over the left hip and cannot bear weight. He tells you he does not remember falling. He has been unable to reach the phone.

Which two medications on that counter change your thinking most?

choices.text: Warfarin, because a fall with anticoagulation risks a large occult bleed, and prednisone, because chronic steroids mean he cannot mount a cortisol stress response
choices.feedback: Exactly the two. Anticoagulated older adults bleed into hips, retroperitoneum and head with minor trauma. Chronic steroids put adrenal crisis on the list for any hypotension that does not answer fluid, and they also explain the low glucose.

choices.text: Metoprolol and warfarin, because both directly cause hypoglycemia
choices.feedback: Half right on relevance, wrong on mechanism. Neither drug is a typical cause of hypoglycemia. Metoprolol matters because it masks tachycardia; warfarin matters because of bleeding risk.

choices.text: None of them; the medication list can wait for the hospital
choices.feedback: Wrong. This list rewrites the assessment: one drug masks a vital sign, one multiplies bleeding risk, and one disables the stress response. It is a two-minute read that changes the plan.

choices.text: Prednisone alone, because steroids explain the confusion
choices.feedback: Incomplete. Prednisone is critically relevant, but for adrenal crisis risk and hypoglycemia rather than as a direct cause of confusion, and ignoring the warfarin leaves a bleeding risk unconsidered.

steps.prompt:
En route you warm him and give oral glucose, which he takes. Repeat glucose is `104 mg/dL`, but he remains confused and his pressure has drifted.

He has now received `1 L` of isotonic fluid with no improvement in pressure.

choices.text: Recite the fluid-unresponsive hypotension list out loud: ongoing bleeding, obstruction, pump failure, vasodilation, and adrenal crisis, and flag the prednisone to the receiving team
choices.feedback: This is the move. All five deserve consideration here, and two are strongly in play: occult bleeding on warfarin from the fall, and adrenal crisis from chronic steroids. Naming the steroid history is the item most often missed.

choices.text: Give a second liter and reassess without changing the working diagnosis
choices.feedback: Fluid is reasonable, but repeating an intervention that has already failed without revisiting the differential is how the steroid history and the bleed get missed. Treat and rethink at the same time.

choices.text: Assume the pressure drop is from rewarming vasodilation and take no further action
choices.feedback: Rewarming can drop pressure, but writing off a 20-point fall in an anticoagulated fall patient on chronic steroids as expected is exactly the assumption this case punishes.

choices.text: Withhold further fluid entirely since it has not worked
choices.feedback: Harmful. Fluid not producing an adequate response is a reason to broaden the differential, not to stop resuscitating a hypotensive patient.

steps.prompt:
At the hospital the team asks for your handoff. You have about thirty seconds before they start their own assessment.

What goes in it?

choices.text: Down two days in a cold house, new confusion from a sharp baseline, temp 35.4 on arrival, glucose 62 corrected to 104, hip injury on warfarin, chronic prednisone 10 mg daily, 1 L fluid with no pressure response, and he is beta-blocked so the rate is unreliable
choices.feedback: Complete and correctly prioritized. Every element changes a decision: the baseline for the confusion, the steroid history for adrenal crisis, the warfarin for the bleed, and the beta blocker for why the heart rate is not telling anyone anything.

choices.text: 81-year-old found down, vitals stable, possible hip fracture
choices.feedback: Inadequate and misleading. Calling a hypotensive, tachypneic, confused, anticoagulated, steroid-dependent patient stable buries every finding that matters.

choices.text: Give the vital signs only and let the team ask follow-up questions
choices.feedback: Insufficient. The vitals are the least informative part of this case precisely because they are pharmacologically masked. The history is what carries the risk.

choices.text: Lead with the hip injury and mention the medications only if asked
choices.feedback: Wrong order. The hip is visible and will be found; the steroid history and the unresponsive hypotension are what a busy team can miss if you do not say them.

scenarios.debrief:
This case is about masked warning systems. Age blunted his sympathetic response, metoprolol blocked the tachycardia, immunosenescence removed the fever, and chronic prednisone removed the cortisol stress response. Four of the signals you normally rely on were disabled before you walked in.

What was left still told the story: new confusion against a sharp baseline, a respiratory rate of 22 rising to 26, a temperature below 36 C, and hypotension that did not answer a liter of fluid.

Two lists are worth carrying from here. The fluid-unresponsive hypotension differential, which is ongoing bleeding, obstruction, pump failure, vasodilation and adrenal crisis. And the three questions for every older patient: what is their baseline mental status, what is their usual blood pressure, and what are they taking. On this call the answer to the third question, prednisone 10 mg daily, was sitting in plain view on the counter.
